title: Mitosis
content:
# Mitosis

## Learning Objectives
By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:
- Define mitosis and explain its purpose
- Describe the stages of mitosis
- Explain the importance of mitosis for growth, repair, and asexual reproduction
- Compare the daughter cells produced by mitosis to the parent cell

## Introduction

**Mitosis** is a type of cell division that produces two genetically identical daughter cells from one parent cell. It is essential for growth, repair, and asexual reproduction in organisms.

Before a cell can divide, it must copy all of its DNA so that each daughter cell receives a complete set of genetic information.

## Key Concepts

### Why Do Cells Divide?

Cells divide for three main reasons:

1. **Growth** - Organisms grow by producing more cells through mitosis
2. **Repair** - Damaged tissues are replaced by new cells
3. **Asexual reproduction** - Some organisms reproduce by mitosis alone, producing genetically identical offspring (clones)

### Key Features of Mitosis

| Feature | Detail |
|---------|--------|
| Number of divisions | 1 |
| Daughter cells produced | 2 |
| Chromosome number | Same as parent cell (diploid remains diploid) |
| Genetic variation | None - daughter cells are genetically identical |
| Where it occurs | All body cells (somatic cells) |
| Purpose | Growth, repair, asexual reproduction |

### Chromosomes and DNA Replication

Before mitosis can occur, the DNA must be copied. This happens during **interphase** (the stage before mitosis).

**Key terms:**
- **Chromosome** - A structure made of DNA, carrying genetic information
- **Chromatid** - One copy of a duplicated chromosome, joined to its sister chromatid
- **Sister chromatids** - Two identical copies of a chromosome, joined at the centromere
- **Centromere** - The point where sister chromatids are joined

[DIAGRAM: A chromosome showing sister chromatids joined at the centromere]

After DNA replication, each chromosome consists of two identical sister chromatids joined at the centromere.

### The Stages of Mitosis

Mitosis is a continuous process but is divided into four main stages for easier study:

[DIAGRAM: Four stages of mitosis in an animal cell, showing chromosome behaviour]

#### 1. Prophase

**What happens:**
- Chromosomes condense (shorten and thicken), becoming visible
- Each chromosome is seen as two sister chromatids joined at the centromere
- The nuclear membrane (envelope) breaks down
- Centrioles move to opposite poles of the cell (in animal cells)
- Spindle fibres begin to form

[DIAGRAM: Cell in prophase showing condensed chromosomes and breaking nuclear membrane]

#### 2. Metaphase

**What happens:**
- Chromosomes line up along the middle (equator) of the cell
- Spindle fibres attach to the centromere of each chromosome
- Chromosomes are arranged in a single plane
- This is the best stage to count chromosomes

[DIAGRAM: Cell in metaphase showing chromosomes aligned at the equator]

#### 3. Anaphase

**What happens:**
- The centromere divides
- Sister chromatids separate (they are now called chromosomes)
- Spindle fibres shorten, pulling chromosomes to opposite poles
- The cell begins to elongate
- The separated chromosomes are pulled centromere-first

[DIAGRAM: Cell in anaphase showing separated chromosomes moving to poles]

#### 4. Telophase

**What happens:**
- Chromosomes arrive at opposite poles
- Chromosomes decondense (uncoil and become less visible)
- Nuclear membranes reform around each set of chromosomes
- Spindle fibres break down
- Two nuclei are now present in the cell

[DIAGRAM: Cell in telophase showing two new nuclei forming]

### Cytokinesis

After mitosis (nuclear division), the cytoplasm divides in a process called **cytokinesis**.

**In animal cells:**
- The cell membrane pinches inward (cleavage furrow)
- The cell "pinches" in two from the outside

**In plant cells:**
- A cell plate forms in the middle
- A new cell wall develops down the middle
- The cell divides from the inside out

[DIAGRAM: Cytokinesis in animal cell vs plant cell]

### Summary Table of Mitosis Stages

| Stage | Main Events |
|-------|------------|
| Prophase | Chromosomes condense, nuclear membrane breaks down, spindle forms |
| Metaphase | Chromosomes line up at equator, spindle fibres attach |
| Anaphase | Sister chromatids separate, move to opposite poles |
| Telophase | Chromosomes decondense, nuclear membranes reform |
| Cytokinesis | Cytoplasm divides, two daughter cells form |

**Memory aid: PMAT** (Prophase, Metaphase, Anaphase, Telophase)

### The Importance of Mitosis

#### For Growth
When you grow from a baby to an adult, your body produces trillions of new cells through mitosis. Each new cell is genetically identical, ensuring your body develops correctly.

#### For Repair
When you cut your skin, cells around the wound divide by mitosis to produce new cells that heal the wound. The new cells are identical to the original skin cells.

#### For Asexual Reproduction
Organisms like bacteria (binary fission), yeast (budding), strawberry plants (runners), and potatoes (tubers) can reproduce using mitosis. The offspring are genetically identical clones of the parent.

### Chromosome Numbers

In humans:
- Body cells have 46 chromosomes (23 pairs) - this is the **diploid** number (2n)
- After mitosis, each daughter cell has 46 chromosomes
- The chromosome number stays the same

$$\text{Parent cell: 46 chromosomes} \rightarrow \text{2 daughter cells: 46 chromosomes each}$$

## Practical Applications

### Cancer
- Cancer occurs when cell division becomes uncontrolled
- Normal controls on the cell cycle fail
- Cells divide continuously, forming tumours
- Understanding mitosis helps develop cancer treatments

### Tissue Engineering
- Scientists use mitosis to grow new tissues
- Skin grafts for burn victims
- Growing organs for transplant (research)

## Common Exam Questions

- Describe the stages of mitosis
- State the number of daughter cells produced and their chromosome number
- Explain why mitosis is important for growth/repair
- Compare mitosis with meiosis (see later lesson)

## Common Misconceptions

- **Misconception:** Mitosis and cell division are the same thing
- **Reality:** Mitosis is the division of the nucleus; cytokinesis is the division of the whole cell. Together they make up cell division.

- **Misconception:** Mitosis produces genetic variation
- **Reality:** Mitosis produces genetically identical cells. Only meiosis (and mutations) produce genetic variation.

- **Misconception:** Mitosis only happens for growth
- **Reality:** Mitosis is also essential for repair and asexual reproduction.

- **Misconception:** Chromosomes double during mitosis
- **Reality:** DNA replication (chromosome doubling) happens during interphase, BEFORE mitosis begins.

## Practice Questions

1. State the number of daughter cells produced by mitosis. (1 mark)

2. Name the stage of mitosis where chromosomes line up in the middle of the cell. (1 mark)

3. Explain why mitosis is important for wound healing. (2 marks)

4. A human body cell has 46 chromosomes. How many chromosomes will be in each daughter cell after mitosis? Explain your answer. (3 marks)

5. Describe what happens to the chromosomes during prophase and metaphase. (4 marks)

6. Describe the stages of mitosis, starting from when the chromosomes have already been copied. (6 marks)

## Key Terms Glossary

| Term | Definition |
|------|------------|
| Mitosis | Type of cell division producing two genetically identical daughter cells |
| Interphase | Stage before mitosis where DNA replicates |
| Chromosome | Structure made of DNA carrying genetic information |
| Sister chromatids | Two identical copies of a chromosome joined at the centromere |
| Centromere | Point where sister chromatids are joined |
| Spindle fibres | Protein fibres that move chromosomes during mitosis |
| Cytokinesis | Division of the cytoplasm after mitosis |
| Diploid | Having two complete sets of chromosomes (2n) |
| Clone | Genetically identical organism or cell |

## Summary

- Mitosis produces two genetically identical daughter cells
- It occurs in four stages: prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase (PMAT)
- DNA replicates during interphase before mitosis begins
- Mitosis is essential for growth, repair, and asexual reproduction
- The chromosome number stays the same after mitosis
- Cytokinesis follows mitosis to divide the cytoplasm
